questions.question: A plant turns much of the glucose its leaves make into starch, long chains of glucose packed into grains, and stores it in its roots, seeds and tubers. Why does the plant keep its store as starch rather than as the glucose itself?
questions.answer: Packed in grains, it draws no extra water into the cells
choices: Packed in grains, it draws no extra water into the cells
Packed in grains, it also builds the walls of the cells
Packed in grains, it gives energy without being broken down
Packed in grains, it travels easily to the rest of the plant
questions.context: Glucose dissolved in a cell's water would add to what is dissolved inside, and water would flow in by osmosis until the cell swelled; starch does not dissolve, so a plant can pack a great deal of it away without upsetting its water balance. The plant breaks starch back into glucose when it needs the energy, and its sugar travels as sucrose, not starch. Its cell walls are cellulose, another chain of glucose, whose links let the chains lie straight and bind into strong fibres.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology compares the jobs of the large molecules and ties them to osmosis, and why a plant stores starch rather than sugar is the standard case.

questions.question: The human body keeps a short-term energy store of glycogen, a branched chain of glucose, in the liver and muscles. It keeps a far larger long-term store as fat, in its fat cells. Why does fat suit the long-term store?
questions.answer: Gram for gram, it packs in far more energy
choices: Gram for gram, it packs in far more energy
Gram for gram, it gives up its energy faster
Gram for gram, it dissolves more readily in blood
Gram for gram, it holds more water for the cells
questions.context: A gram of fat holds more than twice the energy of a gram of glycogen, and fat is stored dry, while each gram of glycogen is held with three or four grams of water. Glycogen is the quick store, broken down fast when the body suddenly needs glucose, and the liver's supply lasts only half a day to a day. Fat does not dissolve in water, so the blood carries it wrapped in protein packages called lipoproteins.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that lipids are the cell's long-term energy store and carbohydrates its quick one, and asks why.

questions.question: Ernest Overton put living cells into solutions of about 500 different substances in the 1890s and measured how readily each one got inside. Substances that dissolve in fats and oils got in far more readily than those that dissolve only in water. What did he conclude about the cell's outer boundary?
questions.answer: It is a thin layer made largely of fatty material
choices: It is a thin layer made largely of fatty material
It is a fine sieve that lets in only small molecules
It is the stiff cell wall, built of tough fibres
It is a pump that pulls in whatever dissolves in oil
questions.context: A fatty barrier lets through what mixes with fat, as oil mixes with oil, so the easy entry of fat-soluble substances, large or small, pointed to a boundary made largely of fat; he guessed it held lecithin, a phospholipid, and cholesterol. Size was not the rule that a sieve would follow, and his work also told the plant cell wall apart from the membrane inside it. Such substances slip through by diffusion, with no pumping.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that the cell membrane is made of lipids, and Overton's permeability tests are the first evidence for it.

questions.question: Evert Gorter and François Grendel took red blood cells from people and several other mammals in 1925. A mammal's mature red blood cell has no nucleus and no inner membranes. The two men dissolved the fat out of the cells, spread it on water as a film one molecule thick and found that it covered about twice the cells' total surface. What did they conclude about the cell membrane?
questions.answer: It is a double layer of fat molecules
choices: It is a double layer of fat molecules
It is a single layer of fat molecules
It is fat on one face and protein on the other
It holds only half the cell's fat, the rest lying inside
questions.context: With no inner membranes, all of a red blood cell's fat lies in its outer membrane, so a film that covers twice the cells' surface means the fat around each cell is stacked two molecules deep. Each phospholipid's water-loving head faces the watery fluid on one side or the other, and its two oily tails turn inward. Their solvent missed about a quarter of the fat and their measurements made the cells look smaller than they are, but the two errors roughly cancelled, and the double layer has stood.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches the phospholipid bilayer, and Gorter and Grendel's red-cell film is the classic experiment that found it.

questions.question: Proteins do much of the work in living things, as enzymes, in the muscle that contracts, as the keratin of hair and as antibodies. Frederick Sanger spent from 1943 to 1955 on insulin, a small protein from cattle. He broke its chains into short pieces in several ways, found the order of amino acids in each piece and fitted the overlapping pieces together. What did his finished result show about a protein?
questions.answer: It is a chain of amino acids in one exact order
choices: It is a chain of amino acids in one exact order
It is a mix of chains that vary from molecule to molecule
It is a chain of amino acids repeating one short pattern
It is a chain of sugars with amino acids hung along it
questions.context: Insulin turned out to be two chains, of 21 and 30 amino acids, each in a fixed order, and by extension every kind of protein has its own exact sequence; many chemists had thought proteins somewhat shapeless. A chain folds into a shape set by that order, and the shape fits the protein for its job. Sanger won a Nobel Prize for the work in 1958.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that a protein is a chain of amino acids whose sequence sets its shape and job, and Sanger's insulin is the first protein ever sequenced.

questions.question: Friedrich Miescher found deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) in white blood cells in the 1860s, and Phoebus Levene later showed that it is a chain built from four kinds of nucleotide. A protein is a chain too, built from about 20 kinds of amino acid. Into the 1940s, most biologists expected genes to be made of protein. Why did protein seem the likelier material?
questions.answer: More kinds of unit could make far more different chains
choices: More kinds of unit could make far more different chains
More kinds of unit could store more energy in each chain
More kinds of unit could make each chain harder to break
More kinds of unit could let each chain copy itself
questions.context: Genes must carry a vast store of varied instructions, and twenty kinds of unit seemed to promise far more variety than four; Levene even took DNA for a plain repeat of its four nucleotides, chemically far too simple to carry genes. Experiments in 1944 and 1952 showed that genes are DNA after all, and Erwin Chargaff found that its four nucleotides are not present in equal amounts. Strung in any order along a very long chain, four kinds of unit can spell out endless different messages, and ribonucleic acid (RNA) carries copies of them to where proteins are built.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that nucleic acids carry a cell's information, and the long expectation that genes were protein is the standard story of how that was found.

questions.question: A cell in the human body holds about 30 times as much potassium as the fluid around it. Potassium leaks slowly out through its membrane all the time by diffusion, from more crowded to less, yet the difference lasts. Which observation would show that the cell keeps the difference up by active transport?
questions.answer: A poison that cuts off its energy supply lets the difference fade
choices: A poison that cuts off its energy supply lets the difference fade
A tear made in its membrane lets the difference fade
Warming the cell makes the potassium leak out faster
More potassium in the fluid outside slows the leak
questions.context: Active transport spends the cell's energy to carry a substance against the crowd, from less to more, so cutting off the energy lets the leak win and the difference runs down; poisons such as cyanide stop it in just this way. A tear, warmth or extra potassium outside each changes the leak, which is diffusion and needs no energy. The pump that carries potassium in and sodium out was found by Jens Christian Skou in crab nerves in 1957, and it uses a large share of the energy many cells spend.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to tell diffusion from active transport, and the test of cutting off a cell's energy is how the difference is shown.

questions.question: Jean-Antoine Nollet sealed alcohol inside a piece of pig's bladder in 1748 and set it in water. The bladder swelled, and in some trials it burst. Henri Dutrochet, a French doctor, gave the process its name in the 1820s. Why did the bladder swell?
questions.answer: Its wall let water in far more readily than alcohol out
choices: Its wall let water in far more readily than alcohol out
Its wall let alcohol out far more readily than water in
The alcohol turned to vapour and pressed the wall outward
The alcohol soaked into the wall and made it stretch
questions.context: Water crossed the bladder into the alcohol while the alcohol stayed trapped inside, so the bladder filled until it was tight. Dutrochet's words endosmose and exosmose are the roots of the word osmosis: water moving through a membrane toward the side with more of other substances mixed in. A raisin dropped in water swells the same way, as water passes in through its skin toward the sugar inside.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches osmosis as water crossing a selectively permeable membrane, and Nollet's bladder is the first recorded case.

questions.question: Salt sprinkled on a garden slug makes it pour out slime and shrivel, and it dies within minutes. Salt on a person's hand does no such harm. What makes the difference?
questions.answer: Its skin lets water pass out very easily
choices: Its skin lets water pass out very easily
Its slime reacts with the salt to form a poison
Its skin soaks up the salt, which poisons its cells
Its soft skin is cut by the sharp grains of salt
questions.context: Salt dissolves in the slug's slime, making a brine saltier than the inside of its body, and water flows out of its skin cells toward the salt by osmosis until it dies of drying out; Gordon Port of Newcastle University says no chemical reaction is involved. A person's skin lets far less water through. Red blood cells in strong salt water shrink the same way, and in pure water they swell and can burst.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology applies osmosis to living things, and the slug in salt is the textbook case of water drawn out of cells.
